title: Cab booking model and matching
idea: A cab booking low-level design (LLD) models riders, drivers, vehicles and ride requests, then matches each request to the nearest free driver of the right type, exactly once.

analogy.text: A taxi-rank dispatcher looks at the free cars, picks the closest one of the right size, and radios "that car is yours" before taking the next call.
analogy.breaks: A dispatcher sees the street; your matcher sees only reported coordinates.

points: Nouns become classes: `Driver`, `RideRequest`, `Location`, `VehicleType`; verbs become services.
`NearestDriverMatcher` only ranks candidates: filter by type and radius, then sort by distance.
`DriverRegistry` owns availability; `tryReserve` checks and takes a driver in one atomic step.
In interviews, call the matcher a strategy: ETA or rating ranking plugs in.

hero.title: One sedan request finds its driver

steps.caption: Rider A sends a `RideRequest`: pickup point plus vehicle type. Nothing is assigned yet.
The service passes the request and a snapshot of free drivers to the matcher.
`D1` is close but rides a bike. The type filter drops it first.
`D2` is a sedan, but outside the 5 km radius. The radius filter drops it.
The survivors are sorted by distance, ties broken by id. `D3` ranks first.
The service calls `tryReserve`. The registry removes `D3` from the free set in one locked step.
Rider B asks next. `D3` is no longer free, so `D4` is ranked and reserved.
Rider C finds no sedan in range. The service answers "no driver" instead of a far or wrong car.

code.title: The problem: first free driver
code.caption: Matching by list order: wrong vehicle, one driver sent to two riders, and a far car chosen.

walk.text: Returns the first driver with the flag set. Vehicle type and distance are never checked.
Nothing flips `available`, so riders A and B both get the same bike.
Adding a type check helps, but list order still beats distance: `D2` wins over a nearer `D3`.
`location` and `available` are package-private, so any class can flip them. Two threads could both read true.
`Location` is the one good part: an immutable record with its own distance method.

code.title: The fix: rank, then reserve
code.caption: A matcher ranks candidates; a registry hands each driver out once. The service only coordinates.

walk.text: Value objects are records. A driver who moves gets a new `Driver` record, not a mutated one.
The matcher contract returns a ranked list, best first. It does not reserve anything.
Filter by type and radius, sort by distance, break ties by id so the result is stable.
The registry owns the free set. `synchronized` makes check-and-take atomic across threads.
If another request grabbed the top driver first, `tryReserve` fails and the loop tries the next.
An empty ranking is a normal outcome, not an exception. The caller can retry or widen the radius.

pitfalls: Matching inside `Driver` or `Rider` creates a god class; keep ranking in a separate matcher.
Checking `isAvailable()` then setting it in two steps double-books drivers under concurrent requests.
Sorting on distance alone gives unstable picks for ties; add a tie-breaker such as id.

quiz.q: Same drivers as the fix, but radius 2.0. What does rider B's line print?
quiz.why: `D3` is reserved for A, `D1` is a bike, and `D4` at 3.2 km is beyond 2.0, so B's ranking is empty.

takeaway: Rank candidates in a matcher; hand each driver out once in a registry.

starters: How would I rank drivers by ETA instead of straight-line distance?
How does this registry change when drivers send location updates every few seconds?
What should happen if the reserved driver rejects the ride?
